newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish stocks seen soaring while bonds earthbound.
newsitem.headline: Danish stocks seen soaring while bonds earthbound.

text.p: Danish share prices are seen forging ahead in the New Year, reducing traditional close links to a bond market increasingly seen as past its cyclical peak, analysts say.

Among factors indicating that bond prices are likely to stagnate or slide in 1997, analysts say, are inflation worries and the approach of the 1999 starting date for EU Economic and Monetary Union, which a referendum prevents Denmark joining.

Falling unemployment and rising growth suggest that 1997 inflation could well be higher than the latest government forecast of 2.3 percent and that interest rates are likely to rise again after falling steadily throughout 1996.
"Denmark is further ahead in the economic cycle than much of Europe and may be forced to raise interest rates ahead of Germany," the latest survey by Deutsche Morgan Grenfell says.
Danish voters in a binding 1993 referendum insisted that their country stay out of EMU, although it ironically is now one of few countries meeting the entrance criteria.

Non-membership has added an estimated 0.5 to 1.0 percentage point to benchmark bond yields and concerns are growing that much Danish bond and foreign exchange trade may have to rebase in an EMU member state after 1999.
But analysts believe that the stock market, which has largely shadowed bonds in the past, will surge ahead in the second half of 1997 as its sibling languishes by the wayside.

"We believe that bond yields will rise in the first half and one will see very small rises in the stock market," BG Bank Chief Analyst Fred Fryd Pedersen told the Danish daily Berlingske Tidende on Monday.
"But there is huge earnings potential in Danish industry and when we near the end of 1997 shares will turn out to have risen 8-10 percent," he added.

The Copenhagen stock exchange KFX top-20 index rose by about 20 percent during the first nine months of 1996 and an October survey of analysts saw it rising by a further six to seven percent by the end of 1997's third quarter.
Danish shares, like those on many other exchanges, took a hammering on Friday after U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warned of the "irrational exuberance" of bull markets.
But analysts believe that Danish industry is in such solid shape that share prices will be progressively less influenced by other markets, local or international.

"One should not forget the psychological factor, which in the short term sends shares down if bond prices take a dive. But when players pull themselves together the market will focus strongly on company earnings," Alm.Brand Bank Chief Share Analyst Michael Albrechtslund told Berlingske.
